claim: Due to Imran Khan's criticism of Macron's comments on Islam, French authorities cancelled the visas of 183 Pakistani citizens and deported 118 from the country.
justification: The claim originated from an impostor Twitter account (@PakConsulateFr) with only 469 followers, not the real Pakistani embassy/consulate in France. Pakistan's actual Embassy in Paris (@PakInFrance) publicly denounced the account as fake, and Pakistan's Foreign Office spokesperson explicitly called the story 'fake news' spread by 'dummy Twitter accounts.' No French government source or credible outlet independently verified any visa cancellations or deportations tied to Imran Khan's criticism of Macron.

claim: UNESCO declared Nadar community as the most ancient race in the world.
justification: No UNESCO document, press release, or independent reporting confirms any such declaration; UNESCO does not issue rankings of ethnic/caste groups by antiquity, and even community-history websites making extensive claims about Nadar origins do not cite any UNESCO source. An independent fact-checking outlet (YouTurn) has a dedicated page questioning this exact claim, consistent with it being a circulating unverified/false claim.

claim: More than 225,000 people dead, 225,000. The estimates are, if we’d have acted responsibly, there’d be 160,000 fewer dead than there are today, because of covid-19.
justification: The ~225,000 death toll figure matches contemporaneous data for late October 2020, as Biden himself cited 'more than 220,000' deaths in a related October 23 speech. The '160,000 fewer deaths' claim falls within the range of a Columbia University study Biden cited around this time, which estimated 130,000-210,000 deaths were avoidable, though this was a wide-range estimate rather than a precise figure.

claim: You see the number today? 33.1 GDP. The biggest in the history of our country by almost triple, right? Almost triple. Now it’s very much bigger than any GDP we’ve ever had. You have to go back to the 1950s, and then it’s less than half. This is the greatest number, 33.1 percent.
justification: The 33.1% figure and 'record' claim are accurate, but Trump's 'almost triple' comparison to the 1950s record overstates it — his own White House press release said the new record was 'nearly double' the prior one, not triple. More importantly, the claim that GDP is now 'very much bigger than any GDP we've ever had' ignores that this growth rate followed an even larger record decline (31.4%) the prior quarter, leaving the economy still smaller than its pre-pandemic level, which fact-checkers at the time flagged as the essential missing context.

claim: Wearing face masks will stop the spread of covid 19
justification: Yinon Weiss's actual October 29, 2020 Federalist article argued the opposite of this claim, titled 'These 12 Graphs Show Mask Mandates Do Nothing To Stop COVID,' explicitly stating mask mandates 'do nothing to stop the spread of COVID' and that masks would not meaningfully help with aerosol transmission. The claim as presented misattributes to him a pro-mask position he never held; his article was reviewed by Science Feedback and rated 'Inaccurate' for claiming masks don't work, not for claiming they do.

claim: Jammu and Kashmir (J&K) in Pakistan/India was removed from the United Nations (UN) list of “unresolved disputes”.
justification: The claim traces to a 2010 report about an isolated document that Pakistan's own UN envoy at the time called an 'inadvertent omission,' not a formal removal. Pakistan's Foreign Ministry and UNSC's own annual reports (including as recently as 2025) consistently confirm Jammu and Kashmir has remained continuously on the Security Council's agenda as an unresolved dispute since 1948, directly contradicting the claim it was removed from the UN's list.

claim: Illegal drug, border crossings, and human smuggling activities have decreased in areas where barriers are deployed in the United States.
justification: CBP testimony to the Senate Judiciary Committee confirms a localized reduction in vehicle-based drug smuggling and shifted crossing patterns specifically in areas where barriers are built, supporting the literal claim. However, this creates a misleading overall impression because independent data show over 90% of hard drugs are seized at legal ports of entry (not barrier zones), and experts/CBP data show smugglers largely reroute to unwalled areas rather than being stopped, meaning barriers do not meaningfully reduce nationwide drug or human smuggling activity as the claim implies.

claim: Even if your mail-in ballot is postmarked prior to the Election day but arrives after the Election day it will be thrown out.
justification: Fact-checkers (AllSides, The Dispatch) reviewing this exact October 2020 Facebook post found it to be an overgeneralization: while some states reject late-arriving ballots regardless of postmark, at the time 22 states plus D.C. had grace periods that counted ballots postmarked by Election Day even if they arrived afterward (e.g., Alaska allowed 10 days, California up to 17 days). Because ballot-counting rules vary by state, the blanket claim that a properly postmarked ballot 'will be thrown out' if it arrives late is false for a majority of jurisdictions.

claim: Viral video purportedly shows Pakistani opposition MPs chanted ‘Modi, Modi’ (India's PM)  inside the Pakistani Parliament
justification: Multiple independent fact-checkers (Alt News, AFP/Dawn, BBC, Boomlive, Newschecker) analyzed the original parliamentary footage from Pakistan's National Assembly (Oct 26, 2020) and determined the opposition MPs were actually chanting 'voting, voting' in Urdu, not 'Modi, Modi', while demanding a vote on a blasphemy resolution. Modi's name was invoked later but in a negative/mocking context by the Foreign Minister, not as a chant of support. Fact-checkers specifically identified Shobha Karandlaje among the BJP politicians who amplified this false claim on social media.

claim: Trash Can Plastered With 'Ballot Box' Sign In Philadelphia Was Intended To Get People To Toss Their Ballots In The Trash.
justification: Multiple independent reports (Philadelphia Inquirer, WUSA9 Verify, KYW Newsradio) confirm the 'BALLOT BOX' signs were an advertisement by the Union League Legacy Foundation for a voting-rights history exhibit, not a deliberate attempt to get people to discard ballots. The foundation and city officials called it an unintentional 'messaging blunder' and removed the signs within about two hours; no ballots were found in the trash cans when checked.

claim: Pogba Has Quit The French National Team Over Macron's Remarks on Islam.
justification: The claim originated from an unverified Arabic sports website (195sports) report and was picked up by tabloids like The Sun. Pogba personally and explicitly denied it on Instagram, calling it 'unacceptable' and 'fake news,' and the French Football Federation never confirmed any such resignation. Pogba continued to play for France afterward, contradicting the claim entirely.

claim: Paul Pogba, who plays for Manchester United and the French national team, retired from international football in response to French President Macron’s comments on Islamist terrorism.
justification: The claim originated from an unverified Arabic sports website report picked up by The Sun on 26 October 2020, but Pogba immediately and publicly denounced it as '100% fake news' and threatened legal action, and The Sun itself retracted and apologized for the story. Pogba continued to play for France into 2021 and 2022 (Euro 2020 and beyond), only stopping later due to injury and a doping ban, confirming he never actually retired over Macron's comments.

claim: America went from 75,000 flu deaths last year in 2019 to almost 0 in 2020
justification: CDC data show the 2019-2020 flu season caused an estimated 22,000-25,000 deaths (with a wide preliminary range of 24,000-62,000), not 75,000 — even the worst flu season on record (2017-18) topped out around 61,000-62,000. The claim vastly inflates the 2019 baseline. The 'almost 0' portion has a kernel of truth, since flu activity did drop sharply due to COVID-19 mitigation measures, but this drop occurred mainly in the following (2020-2021) season and did not mean zero flu deaths, as similar viral 'zero flu deaths' claims were separately debunked by fact-checkers.

claim: 5G causes COVID-19.
justification: Claire Edwards did make this claim in an October 2020 video, asserting 5G is 'implicated in COVID-19' and causes similar symptoms to the virus. However, this is scientifically false: COVID-19 is caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus, and multiple scientific bodies and studies confirm there is no causal mechanism linking 5G radio waves to viral infection, with the WHO officially listing it as a myth and researchers attributing apparent geographic correlations to confounding urban factors rather than causation.

claim: Rock musician Jon Bon Jovi performed for 12 people and 7 pumpkins at a campaign event for Democratic presidential nominee Joe Biden in Pennsylvania.
justification: Bon Jovi did perform at a Biden drive-in rally in Dallas, PA on Oct 24, 2020, but contemporaneous local reporting counted roughly 232 cars/several hundred attendees, not 12 people. The '12 people and 7 pumpkins' line originated as a sarcastic tweet/meme amplified by partisan outlets mocking the drive-in format, not a factual crowd count, and the pumpkins referenced were stage decorations at a separate, earlier Bucks County rally that day.

claim: An 'anti-Black Lives Matter' flag replaced the American flag behind President Trump during a Waukesha campaign rally.
justification: Multiple independent sources (PolitiFact, Tow Center/Columbia photo analysis, Milwaukee Independent, Refinery29) confirm that at the Oct. 24, 2020 Waukesha rally, the Thin Blue Line flag replaced the American flag as the sole prominent backdrop, a shift from prior rallies where both flags appeared together. PolitiFact rated the claim 'Mostly True,' noting that given Trump's explicit opposition to Black Lives Matter protests, attendees could reasonably view the flag as an 'anti-Black Lives Matter flag,' though this is a characterization rather than the flag's official designation. One lower-profile source (trumpreporter.net) disputed that both flags were present, but this is outweighed by the consistent, better-sourced reporting.

claim: Donald Trump said that $15 an hour is too much for essential workers
justification: Biden did say this exact line in a Pennsylvania speech on Oct 24, 2020, so the attribution is accurate. However, Trump never literally said $15/hour is 'too much for essential workers' — at the debate two days earlier he said he'd consider raising it to $15 but preferred leaving it to states, and argued a federal mandate would hurt small businesses, not that essential workers don't deserve it. Biden's line is a political paraphrase of Trump's general opposition to a federal $15 minimum wage, not a direct quote or accurate characterization of Trump's stated reasoning.

claim: Joe Biden said he wants to ban fracking in the US.
justification: Biden's official 2020 policy explicitly ruled out a fracking ban, and he repeatedly stated 'I am not banning fracking,' proposing only to end new drilling permits on federal land (about 10% of fracking). However, he did make ambiguous remarks in 2019 and March 2020 debates ('we would make sure it's eliminated,' 'no more, no new fracking') that fact-checkers acknowledged created genuine confusion, so the claim isn't purely fabricated but omits crucial context about his actual campaign position.

claim: 99% of people recover from COVID-19.
justification: Trump did say '99% of people recover' during the October 22, 2020 debate, but contemporaneous fact-checks (NBC News, PolitiFact) rated this false or unsupported, calculating a roughly 97-98% recovery rate among confirmed cases at the time (2.6% case fatality rate). The true infection fatality rate (accounting for undetected mild/asymptomatic cases) may have been closer to 99%, but this depends on methodology and was not what Trump cited; mainstream fact-checkers at the time uniformly rejected the 99% figure as unsupported by available data.

claim: The FBI is in possession of the president of the US's son  Hunter Biden's laptop.
justification: Multiple independent news outlets (NBC News, Fox News, AP, CNN) confirmed by October 2020 that the FBI had seized Hunter Biden's laptop via a December 2019 grand jury subpoena. This was later corroborated by congressional testimony and FBI agent testimony at Hunter Biden's 2024 federal trial confirming the FBI possessed and authenticated the original laptop since late 2019.

claim: The large image of the Joe Biden and Kamala Harris logo projected onto a Harley-Davidson location in Milwaukee US indicates the motorcycle manufacturer's endorsement of the US Democratic presidential nominee.
justification: The projection of the Biden-Harris logo onto the Harley-Davidson Museum building in Milwaukee did occur in October 2020, but this was almost certainly done by outside activists/campaign supporters without company involvement, not an official act by Harley-Davidson. Multiple sources confirm Harley-Davidson has never officially endorsed any presidential candidate and maintains a policy of political neutrality, and the company's own trademark guidance explicitly warns against using its imagery in ways that imply endorsement.

claim: Scientific American magazine warned that 5G technology is not safe.
justification: Scientific American's blog did publish a 2019 opinion piece by researcher Joel Moskowitz titled 'We Have No Reason to Believe 5G Is Safe,' but it was explicitly labeled as reflecting only the author's views, not the magazine's, and Scientific American subsequently published a rebuttal piece calling such 5G safety claims a 'fringe view' at odds with WHO and other health bodies. Presenting this as an institutional 'warning' from Scientific American, as Natural News did, omits this crucial context and overstates the magazine's actual editorial stance.

claim: Officer who wore Trump 2020 mask to polls to face disciplinary action
justification: Multiple independent news outlets (NBC, CBS, BuzzFeed, Miami New Times, Florida Politics, NBC Miami) from October 20-22, 2020 confirm that Miami Officer Daniel Ubeda was photographed wearing a Trump 2020 mask in uniform at a polling place, and that Miami Mayor Francis Suarez, Police Chief Jorge Colina, and Deputy Chief Ron Papier all confirmed the officer violated department policy and would face disciplinary action. Simeonidis's tweet accurately reported an event that was independently corroborated by city officials.

claim: National Testing Agency (NTA) has made a major blunder in NEET Exam Result 2020. They stated that the all India topper had failed.
justification: Several Indian outlets did report on Oct 20, 2020 that NTA had declared a NEET topper as 'failed,' based on student Mridul Rawat's own claims and a Hindustan Times story. However, NTA publicly and directly refuted this two days later, stating the story was 'totally fake, fabricated, and one-sided,' that Rawat's actual score was 329 (not 650), that he was never the ST category topper, and that the emails he cited from NTA were forged. The claim accurately reflects what these outlets reported, but presents as settled fact something NTA itself denied ever happened.

claim: White House coronavirus adviser Dr. Anthony Fauci wrote a 2008 paper that found most 1918-1919 Spanish Influenza pandemic deaths were because of bacterial pneumonia from wearing masks.
justification: While Fauci's 2008 paper genuinely found that most 1918 flu deaths were due to secondary bacterial pneumonia, the paper contains no mention of masks and draws no connection whatsoever between mask-wearing and bacterial pneumonia. Multiple independent fact-checks (Science Feedback, USA Today/Yahoo, CBS/ABC/NBC affiliate VERIFY reports) confirm this is a fabricated addition that distorts the study's actual findings, which attributed the bacterial infection pathway to viral damage to respiratory tissue, not to masks.

claim: Dr Anthony Fauci wrote a paper regarding the Spanish Flu and stated that the majority of deaths in 1918-1919 was because of bacterial pneumonia from wearing masks.
justification: Fauci did co-author a real 2008 paper concluding that most 1918 flu deaths were from secondary bacterial pneumonia, but the paper contains no mention of masks whatsoever, and does not attribute the pneumonia to mask-wearing. Multiple independent fact-checks (Reuters, VERIFY/wusa9, Science Feedback) confirmed the paper never discusses masks, and Fauci directly denied the claim when asked by AP.

claim: Chinese Diplomats Assault Taiwan Counterparts in Fiji
justification: Multiple independent, credible outlets (CNN, ABC, Al Jazeera, AP, Washington Post) confirm that on October 8, 2020, Chinese and Taiwanese diplomats were involved in a physical altercation outside a Taiwan National Day event in Suva, Fiji, resulting in a Taiwanese official being hospitalized with a concussion. China disputes who was the aggressor and claims a Chinese diplomat was also injured, but both sides confirm the physical clash occurred, and a 2022 follow-up report identified one of the Chinese diplomats involved and reiterated that Chinese officials 'responded violently, beating one of the Taiwanese staffers so severely that he was taken to hospital with concussion.'

claim: The Iowa Farm Bureau, US says that it would no longer be endorsing US Republican Iowa Sen. Joni Ernst for her re-election
justification: The claim originated from a fabricated email that circulated on social media, and the Iowa Farm Bureau explicitly and publicly denied it in an official statement on October 18, 2020, calling the email fake and reaffirming its 'full support' for Ernst. Multiple news outlets (CNN, Fox News, Daily Caller, KWWL) corroborated that this was debunked misinformation, not an actual withdrawal of endorsement.

claim: Hunter Biden (son of US president Joe Biden)  had 25,000 pics of him torturing and raping children under 10 in China on his laptop.
justification: The specific '25,000 photos' claim originated from an anonymous internet forum with no evidence, and multiple fact-checkers (PolitiFact, Newsweek) found no credible evidence supporting it. The computer repair shop owner who had physical possession of the laptop stated he did not see child pornography on it, and Giuliani, despite promising to reveal such evidence, never did. While the laptop itself was later authenticated as genuine and contained legitimate material about business dealings, the specific child abuse imagery claim remains unsubstantiated disinformation that spread through QAnon-adjacent online networks.

claim: A third of excess deaths in the United States between 1 March and  1 August 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic could not be directly attributed to the coronavirus
justification: The JAMA study by Woolf et al. covering March 1 to August 1, 2020 found 225,530 excess deaths with only 67% directly attributed to COVID-19 on death certificates, meaning about a third were not directly attributed to the virus. This was independently corroborated by a CDC MMWR study covering a similar period, which found two-thirds of excess deaths attributed to COVID-19 and the remaining third to other causes.

claim: In the US lockdowns are partly responsible for excess deaths not directly attributed to COVID-19 which were observed in 2020.
justification: The Washington Examiner article did make this claim, but independent fact-checks (Science Feedback/Health Feedback) found it 'unsupported by scientific evidence' — the JAMA and CDC studies cited attributed non-COVID excess deaths to undocumented infections and general healthcare disruptions, not specifically to lockdowns, meaning the article extrapolated beyond what the underlying research showed.

claim: It's unclear how Joe Biden acquired his recent wealth since leaving office in 2017
justification: Contemporary reporting from AP, NPR, CNN, and PBS (well before October 2020) documented in granular detail exactly how Biden's post-vice-presidency wealth was earned: an $8 million book deal, dozens of itemized paid speeches with specific dollar amounts, and a $540,000 university teaching position, all disclosed via released tax returns and financial disclosure forms. While some later commentary questioned whether all underlying S-corporation tax details were fully public, this doesn't support the claim that the source of his wealth was broadly 'unclear' at the time.

claim: Hyderabad Metropolitan Water Supply and Sewerage Board (HMWSSB) is delivering 1kg bleaching powder, chlorine tablets to people’s doorsteps
justification: Contemporaneous October 2020 reporting confirms HMWSSB distributed chlorine tablets and instructed/provided bleaching powder to households in flood-affected areas of Hyderabad to disinfect water sumps and drinking water, matching the core substance of the claim. However, no independent source specifically verifies the '1kg' packaging detail or explicitly uses 'doorstep delivery' phrasing, so that specific detail remains unconfirmed even though the broader claim is well supported.

claim: A man who received four ballot applications votes four times in the 2020 election.
justification: I could not locate the specific James Snapp Facebook post, but it matches a well-documented category of 2020 election misinformation that was repeatedly fact-checked and rated false by AP and PolitiFact. Experts confirmed that receiving multiple ballot applications does not allow multiple votes because each voter is tied to a single unique ballot, with signature verification and ballot coding preventing successful multiple voting.

claim: BJP MP Kirron Kher Said "Rape Is A Part Of Indian Culture And It Can't Be Stopped"
justification: A dedicated fact-check (FactHunt) found no evidence Kirron Kher ever said rape is part of Indian culture and can't be stopped; the closest real statement was her saying rape culture 'is not new in India and has existed for ages' while calling for a change in mindset, and an older, unrelated 2017 controversy where she victim-blamed a Chandigarh gang-rape survivor for boarding an auto with three men. The viral quote misrepresents and distorts her actual statements.

claim: A message will be sent to your phone claiming to show that the Covid19 curve is flattening in India, But It will contain a malicious file
justification: Multiple fact-checking outlets (Boom, Full Fact, and others) confirmed that the 'India is doing it' WhatsApp message warning of a phone-hacking COVID curve video was a hoax with no real malicious file, no verified victims, and no credible technical basis. It was a recycled version of an older 'Martinelli' style hoax that had also circulated with other country names like Argentina in 2020.

claim: Saved by the Bell actor, Dustin Diamond died in a prison riot.
justification: Multiple independent sources (New York Times, cancer center statements, medical commentary sites) confirm Dustin Diamond died on February 1, 2021 from stage 4 small cell lung cancer, not a prison riot. There is no evidence he was ever imprisoned at the time of his death or that any riot was involved; the claim also predates his actual death by several months, suggesting it is fabricated.

claim: Controversial abortion methods are allowed under New Zealand's Abortion Legislation Act (2020).
justification: The Act indeed does not name or restrict specific abortion techniques, which is normal for health legislation, but Right To Life UK frames this ordinary legislative silence as if it actively 'allows' extreme procedures like 'partial-birth abortion' -- a loaded, non-New Zealand legal term -- with no evidence such a specific method is used in NZ practice, where late abortions instead typically involve feticide followed by induced labour. This omits crucial context that clinical practice is still governed by professional standards, creating a misleading impression.

claim: IMAGE CLAIMS DONALD TRUMP CURRENTLY FACES A COURT CASE FOR ALLEGEDLY SEXUALLY ASSAULTING A 13-YEAR-OLD
justification: While a real 2016 lawsuit (by 'Katie Johnson'/'Jane Doe') did accuse Trump of raping a 13-year-old with Jeffrey Epstein, all versions of that suit were dismissed or withdrawn by November 4, 2016 — nearly four years before this image's October 2020 claim. No criminal charges were ever filed, and there was no case 'currently' pending against Trump on this allegation at the time the image circulated.

claim: Kanye West was ahead of Biden and Trump in the Kentucky polls in October 2020
justification: Kanye West did tweet a screenshot appearing to show him ahead of Biden and Trump in Kentucky on October 13, 2020, but the data was confirmed by LEX 18 news and the Associated Press to be fake test/mock data from a cached link, not real results or polling. Kentucky does not count early votes until Election Day, so no legitimate results existed at that time, and Twitter flagged the tweets as 'manipulated media.'

claim: Amy Coney Barrett's nomination to the Supreme Court would be confirmed in October 2020, by a Senate majority that represents 15 million fewer people than the minority party.
justification: Barrett was indeed confirmed in October 2020 by a Republican Senate majority that represented fewer Americans than the Democratic minority, which is accurate in direction. However, the specific '15 million' figure appears to be recycled from a different vote (the January 2020 impeachment evidence vote) rather than calculated for the Barrett confirmation itself; independent calculations of the actual Barrett vote found gaps ranging from about 7 million (GovTrack) to 18 million (The Nation), not 15 million.

claim: CNN announces on social media that President Donald Trump dies from COVID-19.
justification: Trump was hospitalized for COVID-19 in early October 2020 but recovered and did not die. Contemporary reporting (BuzzFeed News, Newsweek) documents that fake, doctored screenshots designed to mimic CNN's format circulated on social media claiming Trump had died, but CNN itself never made any such announcement. The claim misattributes a hoax/fabricated image to CNN as if it were CNN's own reporting.

claim: 18-year-old man was recently killed by Trinamool Congress workers in West Bengal for supporting BJP
justification: While West Bengal did see genuine TMC-BJP political violence in 2020 (e.g., the Rabin Paul case in September 2020), no source found specifically confirms an 18-year-old victim killed by TMC workers for BJP support around October 13, 2020. The claim's specific details (age, date, perpetrators) could not be matched to any documented, verified incident in available reporting.

claim: Fact check: Harris' statement on Lincoln's Supreme Court nomination misses key details
justification: Numerous independent fact-checks (Washington Post, USA Today/VERIFY affiliates, National Review, Federalist Society) found that while Harris was correct about the basic timeline of the 1864 Supreme Court vacancy and Lincoln's delay in nominating a replacement until after the election, she omitted the key fact that the Senate was out of session until December (making pre-election confirmation impossible regardless of intent) and that no evidence exists Lincoln ever stated the reason was to let voters decide. Some historians (e.g., in Just Security) disputed this critical framing and defended Harris's interpretation, but the consensus among fact-checkers supports the headline's claim that her statement 'misses key details.'

claim: Daughters of President Muhammadu Buhari and Vice President Yemi Osinbajo brought about the dissolution of Special Anti-Robbery Squad (SARS).
justification: It is true that Buhari's and Osinbajo's daughters posted #EndSARS/#EndPoliceBrutality messages on Instagram around October 10-11, 2020. However, framing them as having 'brought about' SARS's dissolution overstates their role: SARS was dissolved due to days of massive nationwide protests following a viral video of SARS brutality on October 4, sustained public pressure, and government/police action by the IGP -- not because of the daughters' social media posts, which were largely symbolic gestures that even drew criticism from the public for being insufficient.

claim: NASA always receives blessings from the Pope and that God’s permission must be sought before a space mission.
justification: Search results confirm occasional, ceremonial papal blessings and calls to astronauts (e.g., 2011 and 2017), but nothing supports the claim that NASA 'always' receives papal blessings or that God's/the Pope's permission is a required step before space missions. The pre-launch blessing tradition documented in sources belongs to Russian Orthodox priests for Roscosmos Soyuz launches, not a NASA policy, and NASA has conducted countless missions with no papal involvement.

claim: Most Arab citizens support normalization with Israel.
justification: Sky News Arabia's Oct 11, 2020 headline claiming 'most Arab citizens support peace with Israel' was based on a misreading of a Zogby poll: the outlet reported 58-59% support in Egypt, Jordan and Saudi Arabia when the actual figures were 41-42%, having conflated 'undesirable' responses with 'desirable' ones. Independent fact-checkers (CAMERA) confirmed the error, and Sky News Arabia itself corrected the headline days later. Other contemporaneous major surveys (Arab Opinion Index, Arab Barometer) found overwhelming majorities (85-90%+) opposed normalization, confirming the original claim misrepresented actual Arab public opinion.

claim: The PHE has began to combine Covid-19 and influenza statistics to make the numbers look worse.
justification: Full Fact and other fact-checkers confirmed that PHE only began publishing Covid-19 and influenza statistics in the same combined report/document starting 8 October 2020, but did not merge or add together the actual case/death figures. Julia Hartley-Brewer's tweet claiming the numbers themselves were being combined to inflate Covid figures was identified as this exact misinterpretation, and she subsequently deleted the tweet and corrected the record.

claim: From 8th October the UK government will combine weekly flu and covid reports.
justification: Public Health England's official weekly COVID-19 surveillance report stated this was the last standalone report and that from 8 October 2020 data would be published in a combined 'Weekly flu and COVID-19 Surveillance Report' on GOV.UK, a change also confirmed by the UK Statistics Authority and GOV.UK's own publication archive.

claim: Swiss Squash player Ambre Allinckx’s refuses to play in India due to safety reasons
justification: While some 2018 media outlets initially quoted the Swiss coach citing safety concerns for Allinckx skipping the tournament, her parents directly and publicly denied this, stating in an official clarification that 'we, as parent, never were concerned about safety in India' and that the real reason was a family summer holiday. Yogita Bhayana's October 2020 tweet revived this already-debunked 2018 claim, and multiple fact-checking outlets (OpIndia, ThePrint, FactHunt) confirmed it was outdated, false information at the time she shared it.

claim: Labour reversed the 4,400 health health worker cuts by the LNP.
justification: RMIT ABC Fact Check confirmed the LNP did cut roughly 4,400-4,689 health worker jobs in 2012-13, consistent with Miles's figure. However, it found the LNP itself restored most of that cut before losing office in January 2015 (leaving only about 606 FTE jobs, or 3.6 of 8.1 percentage points, still to be restored), meaning Labor only 'finished the job' on a small remainder rather than reversing the full 4,400 cut as implied. The fact-checkers explicitly rated the claim 'overstated'.

claim: WHO ( World Health Organization) approved water, salt and vinegar remedy for coronavirus
justification: Multiple independent fact-checkers (AFP Fact Check, FactCheck.org, Nigeria's NCDC, WHO's own myth-buster page) confirm this is a well-documented hoax; WHO never approved a water/salt/vinegar remedy for coronavirus, and medical experts state gargling with these substances does not kill the virus. AFP specifically identified this exact hoax as circulating in Sri Lanka.

claim: No one lost their health care because of the Wellmark and Iowa Farm Bureau Health Plan Bill.
justification: The Gazette's own Fact Checker examined this exact claim from the same Oct. 8 debate and concluded it could not be independently confirmed either way, finding one BBB complaint alleging a threatened coverage revocation over an undisclosed pre-existing condition, but no formal complaints to the Iowa Attorney General and commentary from the state insurance commissioner suggesting minimal impact on ACA-covered individuals. The claim is technically distinct from the separate, well-documented fact that the plans could deny new applicants coverage for pre-existing conditions, which is not the same as an existing policyholder 'losing' coverage.

claim: it is unknown whether a person under 20 can pass the disease to an older adult.
justification: By October 2020, the CDC had already stated (July 31, 2020) that children of all ages are susceptible to SARS-CoV-2 and may play an important role in transmission, and a CDC MMWR report from October 1, 2020 provided 'preliminary evidence that younger adults contributed to community transmission of COVID-19 to older adults.' This contradicts the claim that it was simply 'unknown' whether people under 20 could transmit the disease to older adults, though the exact degree of risk was still being studied.

claim: China seek for court’s approval to kill the over 20,000 coronavirus patients to avoid further spread of the virus.
justification: The claim originated from a known hoax/clickbait website (ab-tc.com, aka 'City News') with a documented history of publishing false stories. Multiple independent fact-checkers (Snopes, PesaCheck, News Nation, The Print, Khaleej Times, etc.) confirmed there was no such case or announcement on China's Supreme People's Court website, no WHO reporting on it, and no credible news outlet corroboration — the story was universally debunked as fabricated.

claim: Right after a time where we're going through a pandemic that lost 22 million jobs at the height, we've already added back 11.6 million jobs.
justification: Pence's specific figures (22 million jobs lost, 11.6 million added back) closely match contemporaneous BLS/NPR data (22.2 million lost, ~11.4 million added), so the numbers themselves are essentially accurate. However, fact-checkers from ABC News, NPR, and the Washington Post noted this framing was misleadingly rosy: only about half of lost jobs had been recovered, job growth had slowed for three straight months, new layoffs were occurring (airlines, etc.), and true unemployment was likely higher than reported due to workforce dropouts and misclassifications.

claim: U.S. President Donald Trump has suspended all travel from China.
justification: Multiple independent fact-checks (AP, CNN, Washington Post, ABC News) of this exact Pence statement from the Oct. 7, 2020 debate found it false: Trump's policy restricted, but did not suspend 'all' travel from China. It exempted U.S. citizens, permanent residents, their families, and health care workers, excluded Hong Kong and Macao for months, and hundreds of thousands of people (including tens of thousands after the restrictions took effect) still entered the U.S. from China.

claim: Trump said 'there were fine people on both sides' in far-right protests.
justification: Harris did say this at the Oct. 7, 2020 VP debate, and Trump did literally say the words 'very fine people on both sides' regarding Charlottesville, so the core quote attribution is accurate. However, full context shows Trump explicitly said he was not referring to neo-Nazis or white nationalists, whom he said 'should be condemned totally' — a caveat frequently omitted when the quote is used to imply Trump called white supremacists 'fine people,' which fact-checkers have flagged as an important nuance even while confirming the quote itself is real.

claim: Vice president of the U.S Mike Pence said “When Joe Biden was vice president of the United States, the FBI actually spied on President Trump and my campaign.”
justification: Pence did say this exact line during the October 7, 2020 VP debate, so the quote is accurate. However, the substance of the claim — that the FBI 'spied' on the Trump campaign — was fact-checked as false by NBC News and characterized as a 'misleading allegation' by the Washington Post, citing the DOJ Inspector General's report which found no evidence the FBI improperly infiltrated or spied on the campaign and found the underlying Russia investigation was properly justified.

claim: President Donald  J Trump said it [coronavirus] was a hoax.
justification: Harris did say this at the Oct. 7, 2020 VP debate, and Trump did use the word 'hoax' in connection with coronavirus at a Feb. 28, 2020 rally. However, independent fact-checkers (AP, NBC, FactCheck.org, PolitiFact, Snopes, Washington Post) consistently found that Trump was calling Democrats' criticism of his administration's response 'their new hoax,' not labeling the virus itself a hoax — and he explicitly denied the literal claim the next day. Harris's statement, taken literally as she phrased it, misstates what Trump said, even though it echoes a broader and more defensible critique that Trump downplayed the pandemic's severity.

claim: The content of the conspiracy network, Radio Quebec, hosted by Alexis Cossette-Trudel is banned by Facebook.
justification: Multiple independent sources (Radio-Canada, CBC News, HuffPost Québec, and later academic analysis) confirm that Facebook removed Radio-Québec's page and Alexis Cossette-Trudel's personal Facebook page on October 7, 2020, as part of a broader crackdown on QAnon-affiliated accounts. Facebook itself directly confirmed the removal to journalists, and the ban was later followed by similar actions from YouTube and Twitter.

claim: OPCW scenario of the Navalny case is a fantastic story and a planned conspiracy scenario
justification: The Russian Foreign Ministry did make this statement via its official channels on October 6-7, 2020, so the attribution is accurate. However, the substantive claim—that the OPCW's Navalny findings were a fabricated conspiracy—is contradicted by independent confirmations from German, French, and Swedish laboratories plus the OPCW's own analysis, all of which found matching nerve-agent biomarkers, and no credible alternative explanation was ever produced by Russia.

claim: 49 percent of Nigerians are in extreme poverty.
justification: Multiple independent sources around 2019-2020 (World Bank projections, World Poverty Clock) estimated Nigeria's extreme poverty rate using the international $1.90/day line at roughly 47-51%, closely matching the claimed 49%. Nigeria's own national poverty line survey showed a lower 40.1%, but that measures a different (national, non-extreme) poverty threshold, so it does not contradict the international extreme-poverty estimate cited in the claim.

claim: A Congressman Just Introduced A Bill To Remove Nancy Pelosi From The House.
justification: A real resolution (H.Res. 620) to expel Pelosi from the House was introduced by Rep. Ralph Abraham, but it was introduced in October 2019 — a full year before this Facebook post — and never advanced past introduction. Presenting it as something a congressman 'just introduced' in an October 2020 post creates a false impression of recency, and the publisher (AWM America) is documented as a low-credibility site known for repackaging old stories as new, sensational content.

claim: U.S. President Donald Trump has departed Walter Reed hospital just a few days after testing positive for COVID-19.
justification: Multiple independent contemporaneous sources (NPR, Washington Post, PBS/AP, Texas Tribune, Globe and Mail) confirm Trump tested positive on Oct. 2, was admitted to Walter Reed that evening, and was discharged on the evening of Oct. 5, 2020 after three nights, consistent with the claim of leaving the hospital 'a few days' after testing positive.

claim: All students in India who had to switch to an online mode of education due to the coronavirus pandemic are being provided free Android smartphones by the government.
justification: India's official PIB Fact Check unit explicitly debunked this exact viral claim (circulating on Facebook/WhatsApp in mid-to-late 2020) that the central government was providing free Android smartphones to all students, stating no such announcement had been made. Multiple independent fact-checkers (Zee News, India.com, Newsmeter) corroborated this, and some versions of the hoax even contained data-stealing links. While a few individual state governments later ran limited smartphone/tablet schemes for specific grades (e.g., Class XII), there was never a universal national scheme for all students switching to online education as the claim asserts.

claim: Wearing face masks leads to permanent neurological damage, especially in children.
justification: The claim traces to a viral transcript of Dr. Griesz-Brisson's video, which multiple fact-checkers (AFP, Africa Check, ScienceTimes) investigated and found unsupported. Independent medical experts (German Society for Neurology, German Society for Pneumology, Virginia Tech airborne-disease researcher) confirmed masks do not block oxygen or trap dangerous CO2 levels, and no evidence supports claims of permanent neurological damage from mask-wearing, especially not in children.

claim: “Wisconsin Republicans have not passed a single bill in 6 months.”
justification: Multiple independent contemporaneous sources (WisPolitics, Wisconsin Examiner, Ballotpedia) confirm the Wisconsin Legislature's last bill-passing session was April 14-15, 2020, and that it had not convened to pass any bill since then through at least September/October 2020, with one September 2020 report explicitly citing '170 days' without a passed bill — almost exactly matching the six-month claim made on October 4, 2020.

claim: Tax avoidance costs £90 billion per year.
justification: The £90bn figure does circulate in UK political debate (cited in a 2020 Commons motion and originating from Richard Murphy's Tax Research UK estimate), but it refers to the entire 'tax gap' — combining evasion, error, non-payment, hidden economy and avoidance — not 'tax avoidance' alone. Official HMRC data attributes only about £1-2 billion a year specifically to avoidance, with the official total tax gap at the time closer to £35 billion, making the claim's specific attribution to 'tax avoidance' inaccurate even though a £90bn tax-gap estimate exists.

claim: President Trump announces  he has tested positive for Covid-19.
justification: Multiple independent, contemporaneous news sources (CNN, CBS, NBC, NPR, STAT News) confirm that Trump tweeted his COVID-19 diagnosis in the early morning of October 2, 2020, using the exact wording described. The event is extensively corroborated by his subsequent hospitalization at Walter Reed Medical Center.

claim: During a speech on 2nd October 2020 Joe Biden said he would create 550 million new jobs.
justification: Multiple detailed transcripts and fact-checks of Biden's public statements around October 2020 (including his Oct. 15, 2020 ABC town hall, the closest major speech to the claimed date) show him citing figures like 18.6 million jobs (Moody's analysis) and 4-6 million jobs (Buy American plan), never '550 million.' No contemporaneous news coverage, fact-check, or transcript from around October 2, 2020 records any such statement, which would have been a strikingly large and newsworthy gaffe if it had occurred.

claim: US President Donald Trump used a fabricated COVID-19 positive diagnosis to benefit his re election campaign.
justification: The claim reflects a widely circulated but evidence-free conspiracy theory from October 2020. Contemporary reporting (NBC News, spiked-online) explicitly stated there was no evidence Trump faked his diagnosis and no political advantage to be gained, and Trump was hospitalized and treated at Walter Reed, which contradicts the 'fabrication for campaign benefit' narrative.

claim: Flu shots lead to severe or life-threatening conditions making them unsafe.
justification: CDC and independent medical sources confirm that severe or life-threatening reactions to flu shots (like anaphylaxis or Guillain-Barré syndrome) can occur, but they are extremely rare (roughly 1-2 GBS cases per million doses) and the vaccines have an 'excellent safety profile' with hundreds of millions safely vaccinated over decades. The claim cherry-picks the existence of rare severe outcomes to imply flu shots are broadly 'unsafe,' which contradicts the overwhelming body of evidence and mirrors known 2020-era anti-vaccine misinformation trends documented by fact-checkers.

claim: At independence, Nigeria had a population of 45 million
justification: Multiple official transcripts of Buhari's 1 October 2020 speech confirm he stated Nigeria's population at independence was 45 million. Independent demographic sources (e.g., UN-based estimates and ISS Africa Futures) corroborate figures of roughly 44.9-45 million for Nigeria in 1960, matching the claim.

claim: Video shared to make misleading claim that Hathras victim’s family did her last rites
justification: The claim matches the headline and content of a documented fact-check article by Pooja Chaudhuri published on The Wire on October 1, 2020, which reported that a video falsely suggested the Hathras victim's family performed/consented to her last rites, when the family's sister-in-law alleged police staged the scene without their consent. This is corroborated by Zee News reporting the same family allegation, and later reaffirmed in 2024 by Congress spokespersons citing the family's continued insistence that the cremation was done without their consent, contradicting the Chief Minister's claims.

claim: Today, Nigeria grapple has a population exceeding 200 million.
justification: Multiple independent sources confirm Nigeria's population exceeded 200 million in 2020. The UN estimated over 206 million as of July 2020, Nigeria's National Population Commission estimated 206.3 million, and World Bank data shows 206,139,600 for 2020. Africa Check's fact-check of this specific speech confirmed the population claim was accurate.

claim: For a cumulative 29 of Nigeria's 60 years of existence as a nation, Nigeria has been under military rule.
justification: Multiple independent transcripts (State House Nigeria, Channels TV, TheCable, Vanguard) confirm Buhari made this exact statement on October 1, 2020. The underlying historical claim is also corroborated by independent academic sources, which calculate that Nigeria's military ruled for 29 years between 1966-1999 (with the 1979-1983 civilian interregnum), matching the president's figure against the 60-year total since 1960 independence.

claim: There has been a 60% drop in government revenue in Nigeria.
justification: Buhari did say this in his October 1, 2020 speech, and it was echoed by VP Osinbajo around the same time, so the quote itself is accurately attributed. However, independent fact-checkers found the claim 'unproven' because Buhari did not specify the timeframe, baseline, or whether he meant gross federal revenue or retained revenue after allocation to states, and contemporaneous budget data showed oil and gas revenue collections actually exceeding revised targets in early 2020, undermining a clean 60% drop narrative.

claim: There was a 40% drop in oil prices in Nigeria.
justification: Buhari did state this exact figure in his official October 1, 2020 Independence Day speech, confirmed by multiple independent transcripts including the government's own Ministry of Information website. The underlying claim about oil price decline is also broadly supported: global Brent crude prices fell dramatically in 2020 (from around $34-70/barrel pre-crisis to lows near $13-25, later partially recovering to ~$40 by October), and Nigeria's government cut its budget benchmark price from $57 to $30 per barrel, consistent with a roughly 40% decline, though different sources cite slightly varying percentages depending on the comparison period.

claim: For a cumulative 29 of our 60 years of existence as a nation, we have been under military rule.
justification: Official transcripts of Buhari's October 1, 2020 speech confirm he made this exact statement. Independent academic sources corroborate the substance: Nigeria's military ruled for approximately 29 years between the 1966 coup and 1999 (with a brief 1979-1983 civilian interlude), consistent with Buhari's figure out of the 60 years since 1960 independence.

claim: 52% of Nigeria’s current population lives in urban areas.
justification: Buhari's exact statement in his October 1, 2020 speech was confirmed verbatim across multiple transcripts (State House, Channels TV, Vanguard, Guardian). Independent World Bank/UN World Urbanization Prospects data pegs Nigeria's urban population share at 51.96% for 2020, matching the 52% figure almost exactly.

claim: Nigeria’s urban population at the time of independence was approximately 7 million
justification: Buhari's speech text is confirmed verbatim across multiple sources, stating Nigeria's 1960 population was ~45 million with an urban population of ~7 million. Independent Africa Check fact-checking found Nigeria's urbanization rate was 15.4% in 1960, and applying that rate to the UN-confirmed 1960 population of ~45 million yields approximately 6.9 million urban residents, closely matching Buhari's claim.

claim: Nigeria's petrol prices are lower than Saudi Arabia's.
justification: Multiple independent Nigerian news outlets confirm Buhari stated Nigeria sold petrol at N161/litre versus N168/litre in Saudi Arabia, and a fact-check by Africa Check using GlobalPetrolPrices.com data confirmed that broadly Nigeria's fuel prices were indeed lower than Saudi Arabia's and the other countries cited. While experts noted the comparison omitted context like purchasing power and wages, the core factual claim about relative petrol prices holds up.

claim: At independence, Nigeria had a population of 45 million.
justification: Buhari's claim that Nigeria had about 45 million people at independence in 1960 matches UN Population Division and World Bank estimates (45.1 million for mid-1960), and was independently verified as accurate by Africa Check's fact-check of the same speech. Multiple other sources (World Bank data, worlddata.info, ISS Africa Futures) corroborate a figure of roughly 44.9-45.1 million for 1960.

claim: There was a 40% drop in the price of oil, Nigeria's main export.
justification: Buhari did say this in his Oct 1, 2020 speech, and it's true oil prices fell substantially in 2020. However, independent fact-checkers (Africa Check) found the specific '40%' figure unproven and not clarified by the presidency; actual data showed a 36.5% year-over-year drop or as much as 73-90% drop during the worst months, so the precise figure cited doesn't match verifiable sources.

claim: Judith Collins said, on Donald Trump, "actually, he's a damn sight better than any of the other Presidents that have been there before him, including those that you admire, Miss Arden,"
justification: The Spinoff's contemporaneous debate coverage quotes Collins saying almost exactly this line during the September 30, 2020 NZ leaders' debate, defending Trump against Ardern. Social media posts from October 2020 also reference the same remark. Minor wording differences exist but the substance and quote are accurately captured.

claim: There has been a 60% drop in government revenue.
justification: Buhari did say this in his 1 October 2020 Independence Day speech, but independent fact-checkers (Africa Check) rated the underlying revenue-drop claim as 'unproven' due to lack of clarity on timeframe and definition of revenue. Nigeria's own Budget Office data shows actual 2020 government revenue (N3.93tn) was about 27% below the *target* (not a 60% year-on-year drop), and only modestly below actual 2019 revenue (~N4.1tn), suggesting the 60% figure significantly overstates the real decline.

claim: Kamala Harris called Joe Biden Trash.
justification: No credible news source, transcript, or primary record supports the claim that Kamala Harris called Joe Biden 'trash' around October 1, 2020. The only well-documented 'garbage' controversy involving Harris and Biden occurred four years later, in October 2024, and involved Biden calling Trump supporters 'garbage' — with Harris publicly distancing herself from and disagreeing with that language, the opposite of what the claim alleges.

claim: In England You can get a £3,000 fine for not wearing a cloth over your face at the time of this claim.
justification: A first-time offence for not wearing a face covering in England carried a fine of only £100-£200, not £3,000; the higher figure only applied as a maximum ceiling reached after multiple repeat violations under a doubling ('laddering') penalty system. Moreover, by the claim's date (30 Sept 2020), regulations effective 23-24 September had already raised that maximum to £6,400, making even the £3,000 figure outdated.

claim: Covid 19 Will Go Away If You Stop Getting Tested, It's Just The Elderly Dying and People Are Being Intentionally Infected
justification: The claim's core assertions echo well-documented 2020 COVID misinformation that was fact-checked as false: testing more doesn't create the virus, stopping testing wouldn't make deaths disappear (PolitiFact and CNN debunked Trump's similar claim), COVID killed people beyond just the elderly, and the 'intentional infection' claim traces to a fringe article Twitter itself removed for spreading misinformation. However, I could not locate or verify the specific tweet attributed to 'Arthur Brice' on this date, so the attribution itself remains unconfirmed even though the content matches known false claims.

claim: The number of police decline when National Party leader Judith Collins’ was police minister.
justification: An independent AAP FactCheck investigation into this exact claim found that actual (raw) police numbers rose between 2008 and 2016, spanning Collins' two stints as police minister, rating Ardern's claim only 'Somewhat False' after noting a possible per-capita nuance. Since the plain claim is about the number of police declining (not a per-capita ratio), and the raw headcount data show an increase, the claim as commonly understood is not supported.

claim: President Joe Biden is abusing the prescription drug Adderall.
justification: Trump and his surrogate Rudy Giuliani did suggest around Sept 27-29, 2020 that Biden might be using Adderall to explain his debate performance, and Trump demanded Biden take a drug test. However, this was explicitly speculative language ('probably-possibly,' 'maybe') with no supporting evidence, and multiple fact-checks (Newsweek, Slate) confirmed there was no evidence Biden was taking any performance-enhancing drug. The claim as stated presents an unverified insinuation as if it were an established fact.

claim: A “new virus” disease called Novel Bunya V!rus that is caused by ticks is diagnosed as severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS) is spreading in China.
justification: SFTS did spread among tick-bite victims in eastern China in 2020 and was correctly linked to a bunyavirus, so the core epidemiological facts are true. However, framing it as a brand-new/novel virus is false and was even contradicted by the same Chinese outlets reporting it at the time, since SFTSV/SFTS has been documented in China since 2009-2011 and the 'novel bunyavirus' name refers to its original 2010-2011 scientific classification, not a 2020 emergence.

claim: There is more chance of an asteroid hitting Earth on 02/11/2020 than dying from COVID-19.
justification: This was a widely circulated viral claim in 2020 referring to asteroid 2018VP1's flyby around Nov. 2-3, 2020. Fact-checkers found NASA's 0.41% figure referred only to the asteroid entering the atmosphere (not 'hitting Earth' in any harmful sense), and the tiny 6.5-foot object would disintegrate before reaching the surface, posing no death risk. Meanwhile, actual COVID-19 death rates in the US and elsewhere were higher than the percentage cited in the meme, making the comparison false and designed to downplay the pandemic's real risk.

claim: Indian legendary singer Sripathi Panditaradhyula Balasubrahmanyam's family asked the Tamil Nadu government for help to pay the hospital bills after his death, but it was  Vice President Venkaiah Naidu's daughter who stepped in.
justification: SP Charan (SPB's son) publicly and explicitly denied that the family sought help from the Tamil Nadu government or that Venkaiah Naidu's daughter cleared the bills, calling the rumor 'hogwash.' Deepa Venkat herself issued a statement denying she paid any bills, stating the hospital had waived remaining charges on its own. Both primary parties involved refuted the claim.

claim: A child died in Germany from wearing a mask.
justification: This claim matches a well-documented wave of German-language misinformation in late September/early October 2020 claiming children died from wearing masks. German police and prosecutors in multiple regions (Schweinfurt/Unterfranken, Wiesbaden) explicitly denied any such deaths occurred, calling the stories 'Internetmärchen' (internet fairy tales), and medical experts confirmed it is medically impossible for a healthy child to die from wearing a cloth mask. No confirmed case of a child dying from mask-wearing in Germany was found by fact-checkers (dpa, t-online, futurezone/AFP).

claim: A Maryland man was sentenced to a year in jail for throwing parties.
justification: NBC News's own September 26, 2020 article states verbatim that a Maryland man (Shawn Marshall Myers) was sentenced to a year in jail for throwing parties that violated the governor's coronavirus gathering restrictions. This is corroborated by the Charles County State's Attorney's Office press release and independent reporting from CNN, CBS, Fox News, ABC News, Newsweek, BuzzFeed News, and Baltimore Sun, all agreeing on the same core facts: two parties with ~50 people each, conviction on two counts of failure to comply with an emergency order, one-year jail sentence, $5,000 fine, and three years of unsupervised probation.

claim: A Supreme Court nominee has never been nominated and installed while a presidential election is already underway.
justification: Historical records show multiple Supreme Court nominees were both nominated and confirmed during presidential election years while campaigns were underway, including Melville Fuller (1888), Mahlon Pitney (1912), Louis Brandeis (1916), Benjamin Cardozo (1932), and Frank Murphy (1940). Scholarly and journalistic sources from the time explicitly note there is no historical practice of avoiding nomination/confirmation in election years. A narrower claim (no nominee confirmed within weeks of Election Day itself) had more support, but the broad claim as stated is false.

claim: Govt of India is providing money to bereaved families of COVID-19 - Insurance benefits for Covid-19 deaths can be claimed under the schemes of PMJJBY and PMSBY.
justification: PMJJBY genuinely does cover COVID-19 deaths as 'death due to any reason,' but India's official PIB Fact Check and insurance helpline confirmed PMSBY explicitly does NOT cover COVID-19 deaths since they aren't classified as accidental. The claim bundles both schemes together as covering COVID deaths, which is false for PMSBY, and it originates from a site (funds4-covid19.com) that independently checks out as a very low-trust, newly-registered domain typical of COVID-era scam sites.

claim: Jo Biden the U.S Democratic Presidential nominee calls Donald Trump supporters the "dregs of society".
justification: Biden did say the words 'dregs of society' in a 2018 speech, but multiple fact-checks (USA Today, Reuters) found he was referring to a small group of virulent extremists (alt-right, KKK) who oppose LGBTQ rights, not to Trump supporters generally. The viral claim/video circulated by Trump-aligned accounts in 2020 was based on an edited clip that stripped this context, creating a false overall impression.

claim: Nigeria performed poorly in Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) in the past five years.
justification: Independent reporting confirms Michael Ale made this statement in 2020, and it is factually supported: Nigeria ranked 160th-164th out of 166 countries on the 2020 SDG Index, one of the lowest rankings globally, and multiple UN and SDSN sources describe mixed-to-poor progress on SDGs in the years following 2015 adoption.

claim: A mail-in ballot application for voting in the US presidential election which was sent to a deceased grandfather in the State of New Mexico is evidence of potential widespread voter fraud via mail-in ballots.
justification: While an isolated mail ballot application being sent to a deceased person is a real and common occurrence, fact-checkers and election officials consistently attribute this to outdated mailing databases/clerical errors rather than evidence of fraud, and New Mexico has specific safeguards (obituary checks, Vital Statistics reports, ERIC data-matching) designed to prevent such applications from resulting in an actual counted fraudulent vote. Framing a single such anecdote as evidence of 'potential widespread voter fraud' goes well beyond what the underlying fact supports, echoing a pattern of similar viral claims in 2020 that were repeatedly debunked.

claim: Raveer Singh requested Narcotics Control Bureau (NCB) to let him join anxiety-prone Actor Deepika Padukone during drug interrogation.
justification: Republic World and several other outlets did report, citing unnamed sources, that Ranveer Singh asked NCB to let him accompany Deepika Padukone during questioning due to her anxiety. However, the NCB itself officially denied receiving any such request, stating the only communication received was about Deepika joining the probe, not about Ranveer accompanying her. The claim presents unverified source-based reporting as settled fact while omitting the NCB's direct denial.

claim: US President Donald Trump's executive order on September 24, 2020 legally ensures health coverage protections for those with pre existing medical conditions.
justification: Contemporaneous reporting from CNBC, NBC News, KFF Health News, and legal scholars consistently found the order merely declared a policy statement with no enforcement mechanism or legal teeth, not a binding legal guarantee. Legal experts explicitly said it had 'no more legal weight than a campaign slogan,' and even HHS Secretary Azar called it a 'request' rather than a law, while the actual enforceable pre-existing conditions protections came from the ACA, which the Trump administration was simultaneously suing to overturn.

claim: Sunil Gavaskar said that "Virat Kohli has only trained against Anushka [Sharma]'s balls during the lockdown"
justification: ESPNcricinfo reviewed the actual broadcast footage and confirmed Gavaskar said in Hindi that Kohli had 'only practised against the bowling of Anushka,' not 'balls' as the viral quote claimed; the 'balls' phrasing was a misquotation that spread on social media, which Gavaskar denied ever saying, and the social media user who originated the misquote publicly apologized for it.

claim: False Facebook posts claim Philippine vice president demanded multi-billion dollar budget for her office in 2021
justification: Documented budget records show the Office of the Vice President under Leni Robredo had a 2021 budget of about P900 million pesos (roughly $18 million USD), far below any 'multi-billion dollar' figure, and there is no reporting of her demanding such an amount. This confirms that Facebook posts claiming she sought a multi-billion dollar budget would be false, consistent with AFP's typical fact-check framing, though the original AFP article itself could not be directly located.

claim: Adani Logistics Limited has established a food silo in the aftermath of the three farm and agriculture-related bills passing Parliament.
justification: Multiple fact-checks (IBTimes, India Today AFWA, OpIndia) and Adani Agri Logistics' own statements confirm the Moga silo was built under a 2005 FCI agreement and became operational in 2007 — more than a decade before the 2020 farm bills, not in their aftermath. The viral claim linking the silo's construction to the farm bills has been repeatedly and explicitly debunked as false.

claim: Shah Rukh Khan's Kolkata Knight Riders (KKR) is acquiring a 1.28 per cent stake in Reliance Retail at Rs 5,500 crore
justification: The Rs 5,550 crore investment for a 1.28% stake in Reliance Retail was made by Kohlberg Kravis Roberts & Co. (KKR), the global private equity firm co-founded by Henry Kravis, not by Shah Rukh Khan's Kolkata Knight Riders cricket franchise. News reports confirm KKR the investment firm's involvement, with quotes from KKR co-CEO Henry Kravis, with no connection whatsoever to the IPL cricket team.

claim: Due to coronavirus schools and colleges have been closed and because of this, the education of students has been affected. The government is providing free laptops to all the students so that they can complete their education and also give exams with the help of the internet
justification: The exact claim attributed to Isha Biswas was independently fact-checked by Newsmeter, which found it false and noted the accompanying registration link was a non-official blogspot page with no corresponding announcement on any government website. This matches a well-documented, recurring hoax pattern repeatedly debunked by India's official PIB Fact Check unit in 2020 and later years, which consistently confirmed no such free laptop scheme for all students was ever launched by the Indian government.

claim: The Victorian Premier Daniel Andrews of the state of Victoria in Australia accepted a multi-million dollar bribe from the IMF conditional on Andrews locking down the state of Victoria unnecessarily during the COVID-19 pandemic.
justification: No independent reporting, financial records, or investigations support a bribe from the IMF to Daniel Andrews. A nearly identical bribery claim made about Belarus's president was directly and explicitly denied by the IMF at an official press briefing, which stated it does not demand lockdowns as a condition of emergency financing. Pete Evans was a known spreader of unsubstantiated COVID conspiracy theories, for which he was banned from Facebook, and no credible source corroborates this specific allegation about Andrews.

claim: Americans advised to reconsider travel to Ghana due to COVID-19.
justification: Independent reporting (GhanaWeb) and an official State Department-affiliated source (OSAC) both confirm that on September 22, 2020, the U.S. Embassy in Ghana/State Department issued a Level 3 Travel Health Notice advising Americans to 'reconsider travel to Ghana due to COVID-19,' matching the claim exactly in date, content, and source.

claim: Transitioning to 100 per cent renewable electricity generation increase power prices in New Zealand
justification: Collins accurately cited a real ICCC-commissioned modelling result showing a 14% residential price increase, but that modelling was based on an 'overbuild renewables plus batteries' scenario, not the pumped-hydro (Lake Onslow) scheme the government was actually pursuing. Independent fact-checkers (AAP FactCheck via Newshub) rated the claim 'mostly false' because experts, including an ICCC member, said the actual pumped-hydro option was expected to lower prices in the longer term, contradicting the blanket claim that transitioning to 100% renewables would increase prices.

claim: 30% to 40% of Americans will have voted by Oct. 1. 2020
justification: Contemporaneous reporting shows only about 18 million ballots (roughly 11% of the eventual 159.6 million total votes) had been cast by October 15, 2020 — two weeks after the October 1 date referenced in the claim, and at a point when early voting was still just becoming available in all 50 states. This makes a 30-40% turnout figure by October 1 implausible, as it would require 48-64 million votes cast by a date even earlier than when only ~18 million had been recorded.

claim: The recently deceased US Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg was known for her gruelling fitness regime.
justification: Multiple independent sources (CNBC, CBS News, Washington Post via secondary reporting, Politico, and RBG's own trainer Bryant Johnson) confirm Ginsburg maintained a rigorous, well-documented twice-weekly workout regime for over 20 years, including planks, push-ups, and strength training, which was widely publicized during her life and highlighted in tributes after her death on September 18, 2020, just before this tweet was posted.

claim: Trump campaign asked Joe Biden to release a list of potential Supreme Court picks only after Ginsburg’s passing
justification: Multiple independent fact-checks (CNN, KVIA, Legal Insurrection) and contemporaneous news reports confirm that the Trump campaign and Trump himself repeatedly demanded Biden release a Supreme Court shortlist well before Ginsburg's death on September 18, 2020 — including statements on September 9 and September 17, and even earlier at the August 24 RNC speech and a June 22 interview. Biden's claim that the demand only came after Ginsburg's passing was explicitly debunked as false by CNN's fact-checkers.

claim: The family or Justine Damond received a $55 million settlement after she was gunned down by a Minneapolis police officer.
justification: Multiple independent news sources (NBC News, MPR News, FOX 9, Scripps News) consistently report that Minneapolis agreed to a $20 million settlement with Justine Damond's family in May 2019, described as the largest police misconduct payout in state history. There is no evidence of a $55 million settlement figure anywhere in the reporting; the family's original lawsuit sought $50 million but they settled for $20 million.

claim: Flu shot is 2.4x more deadly than Covid-19.
justification: This exact claim was documented by AFP/Medical Xpress in October 2020 as a specific piece of misinformation circulating on Instagram, stating 'Sanofi's flu vaccine Fluzone was 2.4 times more deadly than COVID-19.' Such claims typically arise from misuse of raw VAERS adverse-event report counts, which public health experts and CDC explicitly state cannot be used to establish causation or make valid comparisons between vaccines/diseases. All epidemiological evidence shows COVID-19 disease is substantially more lethal than influenza, contradicting the implied comparison.

claim: MPs are not following workplace Covid guidance by wearing masks.
justification: The core claim—that MPs did not follow mask guidance recommended for workplaces—is well documented and true, but the clearest, most widely reported evidence of this controversy (union complaints, Rees-Mogg's remarks, images of maskless Tory MPs at PMQs) dates from September 2021, roughly a year after the claimed date of 20 September 2020. No contemporaneous September 2020 reporting was found specifically describing MPs flouting mask guidance in the Commons; Hansard debates from that period concerned public-facing mask laws for shops/transport/schools, not MPs' own conduct in the chamber.

claim: Melissa Francis is married to Wray Thorn.
justification: Multiple independent sources, including IMDb biographical pages for both individuals and several entertainment profiles, consistently confirm that Melissa Francis is married to Wray Thorn, with the marriage dated to 1997 or 1999 depending on the source. No source contradicts the marriage itself.

claim: Two Sigma Investments is owned by George Soros.
justification: Multiple authoritative sources (Wikipedia, Forbes, Two Sigma's own official website, and major financial news outlets) confirm Two Sigma Investments was founded in 2001 by John Overdeck, David Siegel, and Mark Pickard, and has always been owned/controlled by its founders. There is no reference anywhere to George Soros having any ownership stake in or connection to Two Sigma; Soros runs a completely separate and unrelated firm, Soros Fund Management.

claim: There is a double standard in how Senate Republicans handled the confirmations for Obama's and Trump's high court picks.
justification: Multiple independent sources (CBS News, NBC, Brookings, Wikipedia, law journal articles) document that Senate Republicans blocked Obama's 2016 nominee Merrick Garland by arguing voters should decide in an election year, then in 2020 rushed through Trump's nominee Amy Coney Barrett even closer to an election (46 days vs. Garland's ~8 months). While Republicans offered a distinguishing rationale (same-party control of Senate and presidency in 2020 vs. divided government in 2016), independent analysts note this justification was introduced only after the fact and contradicts McConnell's original 2016 rhetoric about letting 'the people' decide, supporting the characterization of a double standard.

claim: Photo Showing the remains of Vladimir Komarov, a man who fell from space, in 1967.
justification: Multiple independent sources (NPR/AFP-Getty photo captions, Wikipedia's Komarov and Soyuz 1 pages, and a dedicated fact-check) consistently identify this photograph as showing Komarov's charred remains at his 1967 open-casket funeral, matching historical accounts of his death after the Soyuz 1 crash and the official orders that his remains be photographed before cremation.

claim: Brucellosis is caused by a new virus from China.
justification: Multiple scientific and news sources confirm brucellosis is caused by Brucella bacteria, not a virus, and is a long-recognized zoonotic disease (not new), with documented history and cases going back decades. The 2020 Lanzhou incident that likely inspired this claim was a bacterial leak from a vaccine factory, not the emergence of a new virus.

claim: US Supreme Court Justice, Ruth Bader Ginsburg, fought cancer for decades before she passed away in September 2020.
justification: Multiple independent medical and news sources confirm Ginsburg was diagnosed with colon cancer in 1999, pancreatic cancer in 2009, lung cancer in 2018, and a pancreatic recurrence in 2019, and that she died on September 18, 2020 from complications of metastatic pancreatic cancer. This constitutes a documented multi-decade fight with cancer ending in her death in September 2020, exactly as the claim states.

claim: Wray Thorn is managing director of Sightway Capital.
justification: Primary sources (Milken Institute bio, company press releases, Institutional Investor interviews) consistently identify Wray Thorn as Chief Executive and Chief Investment Officer of Sightway Capital, not simply 'Managing Director.' Only a lower-quality data-aggregator site (Wiza) uses the 'Managing Director' title, suggesting the claim understates his actual, more senior role.

claim: John Cammo was the only one to predict that President Trump would be infected with Covid-19.
justification: While John Cammo's Sept. 18, 2020 tweet predicting a Trump COVID 'infection' announcement is well documented and did precede Trump's actual diagnosis, reporting from the Daily Dot shows at least one other Twitter user (Blue Wyoming) also predicted Trump would get COVID before the actual diagnosis was announced, contradicting the claim that Cammo was the 'only one' to predict it.

claim: English Playwright William Shakespeare’s plays are the work of Amelia Bassano, a black woman who died unpublished and in poverty.
justification: Mainstream scholarship does not accept the Bassano/Shakespeare authorship theory, and there is no solid historical basis for describing her as a black woman. Most decisively, the claim that she 'died unpublished' is directly contradicted by the historical record: Bassano (Aemilia Lanyer) published 'Salve Deus Rex Judaeorum' in 1611 and is recognized as one of the first Englishwomen to publish a book of original poetry, a point explicitly debunked by fact-checkers as 'flatly false.'

claim: The passing of Ruth Bader Ginsburg will have a profound effect on the future of the Supreme Court of America.
justification: McConnell did issue a press release on September 18, 2020 about Ginsburg's death, but its actual text does not contain this phrasing about a 'profound effect on the future of the Supreme Court' — it instead focused on mourning her and justifying a quick confirmation vote for Trump's nominee. While it's true in hindsight that her death profoundly reshaped the Court (leading to Amy Coney Barrett's confirmation and a 6-3 conservative majority), attributing this specific framing to McConnell's actual statement misrepresents what he said.

claim: Canada would like to reopen the border with the U.S
justification: Trump did make this exact statement on September 18, 2020, as reported by CBC News, so the attribution is accurate. However, the substance of the claim -- that Canada wanted to reopen the border -- was directly contradicted by Canadian officials at the time, who reaffirmed continued restrictions, and Canada kept extending the closure for months afterward, with Trudeau explicitly saying Canada was not comfortable reopening due to U.S. COVID conditions.

claim: Turkish-backed armed groups did not commit human rights violations in the Syrian conflict
justification: The Turkish Foreign Ministry did indeed reject the UN's allegations on 18 September 2020, calling them 'baseless' and 'unfounded.' However, the underlying claim that Turkish-backed armed groups committed no human rights violations is contradicted by multiple independent sources: the UN Human Rights Office (OHCHR), the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Syria, Human Rights Watch, and the U.S. State Department all documented killings, torture, arbitrary detention, looting, and other abuses by Turkish-backed Syrian National Army factions in Afrin, Ras al-Ain, and Tel Abyad. A VOA fact-check explicitly rated the Turkish ministry's denial as misleading.

claim: Joe Biden would be the first person without an Ivy League degree to be elected president.
justification: CNN's own fact-check of the town hall, along with Newsweek and other outlets, found that Biden's claim was inaccurate: numerous presidents in the past century — including Reagan, Carter, Johnson, Nixon, Eisenhower, Truman, and Hoover — were elected without Ivy League degrees. Biden would only be the first since Reagan (a 40-year span), not the first person ever, as his phrasing implied.

claim: Nigeria is the leading producer of cassava in Africa and the world.
justification: Multiple independent and authoritative sources — including the FAO, the Central Bank of Nigeria, Wikipedia, and peer-reviewed bibliometric studies using FAOSTAT data — consistently confirm that Nigeria has been the world's largest cassava producer for decades, including in the years around 2020 when the claim was made.
